title: Matrix Formulation of Multiple Linear Regression
text: We express the multiple linear regression model for \(n\) observations and \(p-1\) predictors in matrix notation: \[\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\] where: * \(\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}\) is the response vector. * \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) is the design matrix (with a first column of ones for the intercept). * \(\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times 1}\) is the vector of unknown regression coefficients. * \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}\) is the random error vector satisfying: \[\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}] = \mathbf{0}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n\]

title: Matrix Formulation of Multiple Linear Regression
text: We express the multiple linear regression model for \(n\) observations and \(p-1\) predictors in matrix notation: \[\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\] where: * \(\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}\) is the response vector. * \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) is the design matrix (with a first column of ones for the intercept). * \(\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times 1}\) is the vector of unknown regression coefficients. * \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}\) is the random error vector satisfying: \[\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}] = \mathbf{0}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n\]

title: Matrix Formulation of Multiple Linear Regression
text:
2. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Estimator
We seek \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) that minimizes the residual sum of squares (SSE): \[Q(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^T \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^T (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{y} - 2\boldsymbol{\beta}^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} + \boldsymbol{\beta}^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\]
Taking the vector derivative with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) and equating to zero: \[\frac{\partial Q}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} = -2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} + 2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{0}\]
This yields the Normal Equations: \[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\]
Assuming \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank (\(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) = p\)), the matrix \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) is strictly invertible: \[\boxed{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}}\]

Sampling Distribution & Unbiasedness

Expectation: \[\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}] = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \boldsymbol{\beta} \quad (\text{Unbiased})\]
Variance-Covariance Matrix: \[\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T \operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{y}) \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1} = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\]

title: Matrix Formulation of Multiple Linear Regression
text:
3. The Hat Matrix (Orthogonal Projection)
The fitted values are: \[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}\] where \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\) is the Hat Matrix.

Key Algebraic Properties of \(\mathbf{H}\):

Symmetric: \(\mathbf{H}^T = \mathbf{H}\).
Idempotent: \(\mathbf{H}^2 = \mathbf{H}\) (projecting twice is the same as projecting once).
Trace: \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T) = \operatorname{tr}((\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{I}_p) = p\).
Residual Vector: \(\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}\). Because \(\mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H}) = \mathbf{0}\), the residual vector is strictly orthogonal to the column space of \(\mathbf{X}\) (\(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}\)).

text:
2. Rigorous Regression Diagnostics in R
R provides statistical diagnostic workflows via stats and ggplot2:
# regression_diagnostics.R
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)

# Fit linear model
data(mtcars)
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp + qsec, data = mtcars)
summary(model)

# ANOVA Table
anova(model)

# Extract diagnostic residuals
diag_df <- augment(model)

# 1. Residuals vs Fitted (Checking homoscedasticity and linearity)
p1 <- ggplot(diag_df, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1e40af", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "#ea580c") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Fitted", x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()

# 2. Normal Q-Q Plot (Checking normality of error terms)
p2 <- ggplot(diag_df, aes(sample = .std.resid)) +
  stat_qq(color = "#1e40af") +
  stat_qq_line(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot", x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Standardized Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Cook's Distance (Detecting high-influence leverage points)
p3 <- ggplot(diag_df, aes(x = seq_along(.cooksd), y = .cooksd)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "#0284c7") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 4 / nrow(mtcars), linetype = "dotted", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Cook's Distance Influence Index", x = "Observation Index", y = "Cook's D") +
  theme_minimal()

text:
3. Statistical Modeling in Python (statsmodels)
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Load dataset
df = sm.datasets.get_rdataset("mtcars", "datasets").data

# Fit OLS model with robust covariance matrix (HC3)
ols_model = smf.ols("mpg ~ wt + hp + qsec", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC3")
print(ols_model.summary())

# Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) to detect Multicollinearity
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

X = df[["wt", "hp", "qsec"]]
X = sm.add_constant(X)
vif_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "Variable": X.columns,
    "VIF": [variance_inflation_factor(X.values, i) for i in range(X.shape[1])]
})
print("\nVariance Inflation Factors (VIF):")
print(vif_data)

Let \(h_{ii} = \mathbf{x}_i^T (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_i\) be the \(i\)-th diagonal element of the hat matrix \(\mathbf{H}\).

Prove that \(0 \le h_{ii} \le 1\).
For a model with an intercept term, prove that \(\frac{1}{n} \le h_{ii} \le 1\).

title: Assignment 1: Leverage, Outliers, and Cook’s Distance
text:
Let \(h_{ii} = \mathbf{x}_i^T (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_i\) be the \(i\)-th diagonal element of the hat matrix \(\mathbf{H}\).

Prove that \(0 \le h_{ii} \le 1\).
For a model with an intercept term, prove that \(\frac{1}{n} \le h_{ii} \le 1\).
Compute the average leverage \(\bar{h} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n h_{ii}\).

title: Assignment 1: Leverage, Outliers, and Cook’s Distance
text:
Proof

1. Proof that \(0 \le h_{ii} \le 1\)
Because \(\mathbf{H}\) is idempotent (\(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{H}^2\)): \[h_{ii} = \sum_{j=1}^n h_{ij}^2 = h_{ii}^2 + \sum_{j \neq i} h_{ij}^2\] Since \(\sum_{j \neq i} h_{ij}^2 \ge 0\), we have: \[h_{ii} \ge h_{ii}^2 \implies h_{ii}(1 - h_{ii}) \ge 0 \implies \boxed{0 \le h_{ii} \le 1}\]


2. Lower Bound with an Intercept
When the first column of \(\mathbf{X}\) is \(\mathbf{1}_n\): \[\mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{1}_n \quad \mathbf{X}_c]\] Using partitioned matrix inversion, the projection splits into the mean projection \(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{J}_n\) and the centered predictor projection: \[h_{ii} = \frac{1}{n} + (\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^T (\mathbf{X}_c^T\mathbf{X}_c)^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})\] Because \((\mathbf{X}_c^T\mathbf{X}_c)^{-1}\) is positive semi-definite, the quadratic form is non-negative: \[h_{ii} \ge \frac{1}{n} \implies \boxed{\frac{1}{n} \le h_{ii} \le 1}\]


3. Average Leverage
\[\bar{h} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n h_{ii} = \frac{1}{n} \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}) = \frac{p}{n}\] Points with \(h_{ii} > 2\bar{h} = \frac{2p}{n}\) are standardly flagged as high leverage observations.
